messages.subject: Moderated Correlation Between Two Second-Order Latent Variables
messages.subject_clean: Moderated Correlation Between Two Second-Order Latent Variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a (bunch of) second-order bivariate latent growth curve models for some dyadic analyses I'm running. I'm interested in the correlation between the latent slopes, and in particular, whether this correlation is moderated by the age of the age of the second dyad member.

In the original model, I have code like the following:
"
<...whole bunch of lavaan code...>

Dyad1LatentIntercept =~ 1*Wave1_Dyad1 + 1*Wave2_Dyad1 + 1*Wave3_Dyad1
Dyad2LatentIntercept =~ 1*Wave1_Dyad2 + 1*Wave2_Dyad2 + 1*Wave3_Dyad2

Dyad1LatentISlope =~ 1*Wave1_Dyad1 + 2*Wave2_Dyad1 + 3*Wave3_Dyad1
Dyad2LatentISlope =~ 1*Wave1_Dyad2 + 2*Wave2_Dyad2 + 3*Wave3_Dyad2

Dyad1LatentIntercept ~~ Dyad1LatentIntercept
Dyad1LatentSlope ~~ Dyad2LatentSlope"

I then fit this model with the growth() function. Can anyone point the way to the best way about how to see if `Dyad1LatentSlope ~~ Dyad2LatentSlope` is moderated by `Dyad2AgeAtWave2`?

The following is not correct, but might be in the right direction?

"Dyad1LatentSlope ~~ Dyad2AgeAtWave2 := Dyad2LatentSlope"

Note that Dyad2Age is a manifest variable. I have looked at inprod, but I don't see how it would help with these second-order latent variables. Any and all help is very much appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: Testing inequality hypotheses
messages.subject_clean: Testing inequality hypotheses
messages.body_plain:
Leonard,

Thank you for the clarifications and examples. Super helpful! I decided to first do a chi-square difference test to provide a statistical test of (non)equality of parameters, and then run the goric procedure to assess if the ordered hypotheses are better supported than the unconstrained ones.

Given the bootstrap and the associated computational demands, the iht method is not applicable for me since my model requires about 5 mins to be estimated as is (complex model with N > 1500 using FIML).

Thanks again and all the best!
Jošt

V V sre., 31. jan. 2024 ob 20:43 je oseba LeonardV. <lgf.van...@gmail.com> napisala:

> You can apply the iht() function to evaluate the order restricted hypothesis using hypothesis testing.
> It calls the bootstrapD() function designed for lavaan objects. This results in two hypothesis tests, often referred to as Type A and Type B, as detailed in 10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01565. However, it does not directly answer whether the order-restricted hypothesis holds in the population.
> Moreover, the iht method is really slow for lavaan objects because it needs a double bootstrap procedure. You can speed things up using the parallel option, but
> still don't be afraid to go on a short holiday.
>
> h1 <- 'a1 > a2 > a3; b1 > b2 > b3'
>
> model <- '
>   y1 ~ 1 + a1*x1 + b1*x2
>   y2 ~ 1 + a2*x1 + b2*x2
>   y3 ~ 1 + a3*x1 + b3*x2
> '
> iht(model = model, data = PoliticalDemocracy, constraints = h1,
>     R = 1000, double.bootstrap = "no", parallel = "snow", ncpus = 8)
>
> The advantage of the goric(a) is that you can directly evaluate your order-restricted hypothesis against its complement (i.e., not h1).
>
> fit.lav <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
> goric(fit.lav, hypotheses = list(h1 = h1), comparison = "complement")
>
> From the results you can conclude that hypothesis h1 is 'some value' more supported than its complement.
> See the Vignette in restriktor for "Guidelines interpretation GORIC(A) output" or feel free to contact me.
>
> Leonard

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting CFA results with Ordinal Data
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting CFA results with Ordinal Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jane,

Typically, the results from the robust row (not column) are reported. You can find some information here: Two robust fit measures with MLR (google.com) <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/9umZmFsvX3M>

Note that for WLS family estimators (used for ordinal data), robust indicators are available only since lavaan version 6.13. I think that these indicators are based on the following paper Improving Fit Indices in Structural Equation Modeling with Categorical Data (tandfonline.com) <https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00273171.2020.1717922>, but am not 100% as the lavaan documentation does not specify (only says "based on work done by Victoria Savalei and colleagues"; lavaan.org - 0.6 series (ugent.be) <https://lavaan.ugent.be/history/dot6.html>)

Hope this helps!
Jošt

messages.subject: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.subject_clean: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question about correlated latent exogenous and latent endogenous variables.

Long story short i am wondering is stipulating a covariance relation betwean an endogenous latent variable (therefore its residual part) and an exogenous latent variable allowed.

Explanation:

I am running an extended Theory of planned behavior model of digital piracy. The original model has 3 exogenous latent variables (attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control) and 1 endogenous latent variable (intention).

When i run the original model with the syntax bellow, my model has a good fit. When i run the original model lavaan output gives me an account of covariance between my exogenous variables ATT and SN, ATT and PBC SN and PBC.

model1 <- 'ATT  =~ att1 + att2 + att3 + att4 + att6 + att7
SN =~ sn1 + sn2 + sn3r + sn5r
PBC =~ pbc1 + pbc2 + pbc4 + pbc5
INT =~ int1 + int3 + int4 + int5

INT ~ ATT + SN + PBC'

The model looks like this: https://www.comminit.com/files/tpb.jpg

The extended TPB adds two latent variables PUNISHMENT CERTAINTY and PUSNIHMENT SEVERITY that impact the ATTITUDE variable making it a de facto endogenous variable . The syntax is bellow.

model2 <- 'ATT  =~ att1 + att2 + att3 + att4 + att6 + att7

SN =~ sn1 + sn2 + sn3r + sn5r

PBC =~ pbc1 + pbc2 + pbc4 + pbc5
INT =~ int1 + int3 + int4 + int5
CERTAINTY =~ cert3 + cert4 + cert2
SEVERITY =~ ps2 + ps3 + ps1r
INT ~ ATT + SN + PBC
ATT ~ CERTAINTY + SEVERITY '

When i run this model i no longer get the covariance between the ATT and SN and ATT and PBC. The covariances that the output shows me are: CERTAINTY ~~ SEVERITY, CERTAINTY ~~ PBC, CERTAINTY ~~ SN, SEVERITY ~~ PBC, SEVERITY~~SN.

However, the variables ATT, SN and PBC are heavily correlated in my data and i suspect that the fact that the correlations between ATT and SN and PBC are not included in the model (because ATTITUDE became an endogenous latent variable) severely worsens my model fit.

For example, my model implies that the influence sign of the SEVERITY on ATTITUDE is not what the theory predicts. It implies that for every one unit of reduction in PUNISHMENT SEVERITY the respondents ATTITUDES toward piracy worsen.  Also my standardised residual matrix shows severe model misfit.

I tried testing the following model and the signs in the regressions are what the theory would expect.

model3 <- 'ATT  =~ att1 + att2 + att3 + att4 + att6 + att7
CERTAINTY =~ cert3 + cert4 + cert2
SEVERITY =~ ps2 + ps3 + ps1r
ATT ~ CERTAINTY + SEVERITY'

 I tried searching on the internet and among other papers that used lavaan and the extended TPB and i saw that there are models where the ATITUTE is an endogenous variable but the authors included covariance relations between ATT and SN and PBC in the model syntax.

Given that i am a beginner in SEM i am wondering is stipulating such a covariance between ATITUDE (even if it is endogenous) PBC and SN (exogenous) allowed.

If i include ATT ~~ PBC + SN in my model, my model fit is greatly improved.

When i run the following syntax:

model4<- 'ATT  =~ att1 + att2 + att3 + att4 + att6 + att7

SN =~ sn1 + sn2 + sn3r + sn5r

PBC =~ pbc1 + pbc2 + pbc4 + pbc5
INT =~ int1 + int3 + int4 + int5

CERTAINTY =~ cert3 + cert4 + cert2
SEVERITY =~ ps2 + ps3 + ps1r

INT ~ ATT + SN + PBC
ATT ~ CERTAINTY + SEVERITY

ATT ~~ PBC + SN '

in the covariances section of the output lavaan shows me the covariance between .ATT ~~ PBC and , .ATT~~SN. In other words, i get a covariance between the residual part of ATTITUDE and PBC and SN. I understand why this is i am just interested is this final model syntax allowed.

Sorry if i am not making sense in some parts of my question.

Thanks so much in advance for your answers.

Miljan

messages.subject: Re: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.subject_clean: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Miljan,

I'd say that (a) it is statistically allowed and (b) it is allowed theoretically, if it makes sense theoretically.

A bit of an example from one of my own studies. Lets say I have variables A1, A2, B1 and B2. According to theory, B1 is the predictor of A1 and B2 is predictor of A2. A1 and A2 are measures of a very similar concept, just estimated in relationship to a different person. Now, I have no reason to assume that A1 -> A2 or A2 -> A1, but can justifiably assume that A1 ~~ A2 because they measure the same thing. And although these are endogenous variables, I find it justifiable to introduce a correlation between them. This correlation represents some unexplained common variance between A1 and A2. It is possible that I could measure some third concept that would explain this variance. At least, that is my reasoning.

In your case, I would determine if SN and PBC are reasonably expected to either (a) correlate with ATT but do not determine it or (b) they in fact determine ATT. In case (b) you would then have to specify ATT ~ CERTAINTY + SEVERITY + PBC + SN. Since you note that you found papers that do (a), maybe you can check what their rationale was. Note that without (a) or (b) your model is saying (c) that there is no relationship between ATT and PBC + SN. I find (c) the least tenable.

So, go with whatever makes more sense theoretically, and you can defend it. Probably also best to report and justify it.

Hope this helps,
Jošt

Ps. if you do ATT ~~ PBC + SN, make sure that the correlation between PBC ~~ SN is still there. It's possible that lavaan will exclude this since you manually specified correlations among residuals.

messages.body_plain:
Greeting
maybe this rule be helpful for your problem:

Rule 5

The variances of, and covariances between, dependent variables as well as the covariances between dependent and independent variables are never model parameters. This is due to the fact that these variances and covariances are themselves explained in terms of model parameters. As can be seen in Fig. 6, there are no two-way arrows connecting dependent variables in the model or connecting dependent and

independent variables.

please to p 17 of this book <https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9780203930687/first-course-structural-equation-modeling-tenko-raykov-george-marcoulides>

Hi Jošt! First of all thank you again for your thoughtful answer, I greatly appreciate it and you have helped me immensly.

I am interpreting SEM theory the same way as you, I was just befuddled because I haven't yet seen graphs/models/lavaan code where someone models residual variances between an dependent and independent latent variable.

The models that I found that extend the Theory of planned behavior, either dont show the covariances in their graphs or if they do then, besides regressing additional variables on ATT, they mostly also regress additional variables on SN as well as on PBC, therefore making all of the independent variables from the original TPB model now dependent. Then, when they draw covariances between ATT and PBC + SN and SN and PBC it is a residual~~residual relation (.ATT ~~ .SN + .PBC; .SN~~ .PBC ). This is understandable to me.

Having in mind that my model only has exogenous variables impacting ATT and that SN and PBC not impacted by other variables - If I include covariances between the original TPB latent variables in my extended model where ATT is now basically endogenous I would model a relation between the unexplained part of the ATT latent variable and SN and PBC (.ATT~~SN+PBC; SN~~PBC). As a relative SEM beginner I was very confused is this was allowed, eventhough it was logical in my head to allow for ATT SN and PBC latent factors to covary freely.
Thank you once again so much,
Miljan

On Friday, February 2, 2024 at 4:25:10 PM UTC Jošt Bartol wrote:
> Hi Miljan,
>
> I'd say that (a) it is statistically allowed and (b) it is allowed theoretically, if it makes sense theoretically.
>
> A bit of an example from one of my own studies. Lets say I have variables A1, A2, B1 and B2. According to theory, B1 is the predictor of A1 and B2 is predictor of A2. A1 and A2 are measures of a very similar concept, just estimated in relationship to a different person. Now, I have no reason to assume that A1 -> A2 or A2 -> A1, but can justifiably assume that A1 ~~ A2 because they measure the same thing. And although these are endogenous variables, I find it justifiable to introduce a correlation between them. This correlation represents some unexplained common variance between A1 and A2. It is possible that I could measure some third concept that would explain this variance. At least, that is my reasoning.
>
> In your case, I would determine if SN and PBC are reasonably expected to either (a) correlate with ATT but do not determine it or (b) they in fact determine ATT. In case (b) you would then have to specify ATT ~ CERTAINTY + SEVERITY + PBC + SN. Since you note that you found papers that do (a), maybe you can check what their rationale was. Note that without (a) or (b) your model is saying (c) that there is no relationship between ATT and PBC + SN. I find (c) the least tenable.
>
> So, go with whatever makes more sense theoretically, and you can defend it. Probably also best to report and justify it.
>
> Hope this helps,
> Jošt
>
> Ps. if you do ATT ~~ PBC + SN, make sure that the correlation between PBC ~~ SN is still there. It's possible that lavaan will exclude this since you manually specified correlations among residuals.

messages.subject: Is it possible to create Johnson-Neman plots for second order SEMs with results obtained using the lavaan package?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to create Johnson-Neman plots for second order SEMs with results obtained using the lavaan package?
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to plot a J-N diagram with the results of my SEM where I test a moderation effect (latent moderator, first order construct) between an independent variable (categorical variable, 2 values) on a latent dependent variable (second order construct).

Now I want to do two things:

1.) I want to visualize simple slopes (this I achieve trough jeremy dawsons 2-way interaction excel or R packages). This is something I succeeded in.

2.) I would like to assess the conditions under which the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable becomes significant through the  moderator variable. And THIS is what eludes me. I tried several methods, But I don't seem to understand how you can model a complex latent SEM and use for example the Johnson_Neyman() function in the interaction package for R.

Moreover, I read this article (Lin, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2020.1732826) and this one (Schoemann & Jorgensen, 2021, https://doi.org/10.3390/psych3030024) and the takeaways seem to be that

1.) there is no real method yet (at least not in R)
AND
2.) that this endeavor is not fruitful, because "the J-N technique is of limited value. The scale of latent variables is arbitrary, and determining the specific values of the latent moderator where the simple slope is different from zero is not as useful as identifying how simple slopes change across values of the moderator, which can be accomplished using a simple slopes approach." (Schoemann & Jorgensen, 2021, p.332).

My question is the: should I let go and don't fuss abut J-N plots or is there some sort of work around for that?

messages.subject: Re: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.subject_clean: Covariance between exogenous and endogenous latent variables in SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Balal,

I agree with rule 5, but there needs to be some clarifications. According to my reading of text, the phrase "not model parameters" simply means that these were set to 0 (or some other value) and not estimated. Further, it is usually not appropriate to add a covariance between a dependent variable and an independent variable predicting that dependent variable. So, having y ~ x and y ~~ x at the same time is generally not acceptable. However, there are cases where one would need to introduce such a correlation, such as nonrecursive models, see Kline 2015 Principle and practice of structural equation modeling, p. 136. Such correlations "reflects the assumption that the corresponding endogenous variables [..] share at least one unmeasured cause." (ibid.). It is also acceptable to add a correlation between endogenous variables that do not influence each other, but have the same predictors (see Figure 6.6(b) in the text).

Note however that Miljan's case is different. In that model, ATT is not dependent on PBC or SN, so adding a covariance would be more justified than not adding it. Adding covariance would imply that there is a common, unmeasured cause, and that we control for it. Not adding it would imply that we assume that these three variables are independent (in the population) which I believe is untenable. The only other option is to regress ATT also on SN and PBC, although I doubt that the results would differ much compared to adding correlations.

Hope this clarifies the issue.

Best,
Jošt

messages.body_plain:
You can use parameterEstimates(), as illustrated below:

``` r
# Adapted from the help page of cfa()
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-17
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6'
# Use fewer cases for larger p-values
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939[100:150, ])
est <- parameterEstimates(fit)
# The parameter estimate table
est
```

messages.subject: Comparing path analysis models: mediation vs. (residual) covariance
messages.subject_clean: Comparing path analysis models: mediation vs. (residual) covariance
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I am using lavaan to run path analysis to predict PC from WA and LC. These are multi-group models. Described here is the first step (identifying best-fitting paths); it is  followed by constraining parameters to be equal across the three groups (group.equal = c("intercepts", "regressions")), which is not described here.

My question has to do with the equivalence of models. A reviewer of the manuscript indicated that these three models should be equivalent, but I am not sure. Please advise.

Model 1 models WA and LC predictors separately but allows (residual) covariance.
Mod_1  <- '
PC ~ c(c1, c2, c3) * WA  + c(d1, d2, d3) * LC
WA ~~ LC
'

Model 2 models an indirect effect via WA.
Mod_2  <- '
PC ~ c(c1, c2, c3) * WA  + c(d1, d2, d3) * LC
WA ~ c(a1, a2, a3) * LC
'

Model 3 models an indirect effect via LC.
Mod_3  <- '
PC ~ c(c1, c2, c3) * WA  + c(d1, d2, d3) * LC
LC ~ c(a1, a2, a3) * WA
'

All three models were run with this syntax (models would not converge without intercepts being constrained):

fit<- sem(mod, data = new_df,  group = "grade", missing="ML",
               group.equal = c("intercepts"))

Here are the model fit statistics:

The models appear to be different. I have read that allowing exogenous variables to covary can be equivalent to modeling a path between them (see for example this article <https://doi-org.qe2a-proxy.mun.ca/10.1177/0022219414544544>), but these results appear to indicate otherwise. Plus, in the mediated model, there is only 1 exogenous variable, so I am not sure how that applies to these models.

With regard to models 2 and 3, the only difference is directionality of the indirect effect. The only estimated parameter that differs between them is whether WA is predicted by LC (Model 2), or vice versa (Model 3). Across groups, the estimates of the slopes for WA~LC are greater for model 2 (.25-.32) than LC~WA in model 3 (.20-.23). Given that the other slope estimates are equal across models, I believe the model with greater variance explained will have better fit statistics. Yet, the reviewer indicates that these models are equivalent.

I would appreciate any clarification  about the equivalence of models.

Many thanks,
Jeanne Sinclair

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm conducting measurement invariance tests with ordered categorical indicators across two groups using measEq.syntax() and following up with partialInvarianceCat() to get a sense of effect sizes. The standardized estimates for my factor loadings in partialInvarianceCat() seem quite large and are very different from the completely standardized solutions in the normal model results. I'm trying to understand the cause of this difference and whether I can trust the partialInvarianceCat() results enough to present them.

Here's the code I used to estimate the configural and metric models and to get the partial invariance estimates:

model <- '
L =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6
x1 ~~ x6
x5 ~~ x6
'

model_baseline <-  as.character(measEq.syntax(configural.model =
                              model,
                              data = data,
                              ordered = c("x1", "x2", "x3","x4",
                                          "x5", "x6"),
                              parameterization = "theta",
                              ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                              ID.cat = "Joreskog",
                              group = "g",
                              group.equal = "configural"))

fit_baseline <- cfa(model = model_baseline, data = data,
                        group = "g",
                        ordered = c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4",
                                    "x5", "x6"),
                        parameterization = "theta")

model_loadings <- as.character(measEq.syntax(configural.model =
                                model,
                                data = data,
                                ordered = c("x1", "x2",
                                "x3","x4", "x5", "x6"),
                                parameterization = "theta",
                                ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                                ID.cat = "Joreskog",
                                group = "g",
                                group.equal = "loadings"))

fit_loadings <- cfa(model = model_loadings, data = data,
                        group = "g",
                         ordered = c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4",
                                     "x5", "x6"),
                         parameterization = "theta")

modelsCat <- list(fit.configural = fit_baseline, fit.loadings = fit_loadings)

partialInvarianceCat(modelsCat, type = "metric")

The factor loadings for the baseline model are:

And the standardized loadings from partialInvarianceCat() are

$estimates

I am using a latent growth model to determine the effect of Control Beliefs at time 1 on Conscientiousness, which was measured at two points in time. The code I was given uses both intercepts of Conscientiousness at T1 and T2, both weighted with factor 1, which I don´t really understand, to be honest.

Since my research question deals with the effect of Control Beliefs on the change in Conscientiousness, is it a valid approach to set the weights for Conscientiousness at T2 to 0 and just correlating the Intercept of Control Beliefs with the slope of Conscientiousness?

Does the model still work with Intercept2 set to 0?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The robust version of fit indicators for estimator DWLS and similar was introduced only with version 0.6-13 of lavaan. As it says there (https://www.lavaan.ugent.be/history/dot6.html) it computes robust fit indices only if ALL data are categorical. I think I read somewhere there is a work around (maybe search for it on this forum), but when I tried it (quite some time ago) I still didn't get the robust version.

As for multi group analysis. The output is simply saying that you have to report the scaled/robust chi-square (find in the model output) and not the chi-square that is reported as part of multigroup testing. The warning is because you are trying to compare models with the same degrees of freedom - which is not possible.
Related to the mutli group analysis. In Model 5, although you include Pa ~  Be you still have the same degrees of freedom because you are replacing Pa ~~  Be. For measurement invariance, you are trying to test equality of factor loadings which you don't have (path analysis).

Hope this helps.

Best,
Jošt

messages.body_plain:
You can try semPaths() from the semPlot package. With structural = TRUE, you can print the structural part of the latent variables.

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-17
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semPlot)
mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9
f3 ~ f1 + f2
"
fit <- sem(mod)
dat <- simulateData(parTable(fit), sample.nobs = 200, seed = 1234)
fit <- sem(mod, dat)
p <- semPaths(fit,
              what = "path",
              whatLabels = "est",
              structural = TRUE)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/giMKQ0m.png)<!-- -->

<sup>Created on 2024-02-13 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The plot from semPlot() is highly customizable, thought it would take some time to get exactly what you want.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Is dim_pb3 a data frame or a data-frame-like object, e.g., a tibble?

It seems that sample.cov does not support a covariance matrix in the form of a data frame:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-17
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

dat_cov <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x",1:9)])
fit1 <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 300)

# Convert the covariance matrix to a data frame
dat_cov_as_df <- as.data.frame(dat_cov)
fit2 <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov_as_df, sample.nobs = 300)
#> Error in lavData(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster, ov.names = OV.NAMES, : lavaan ERROR: at least one variance in the sample covariance matrix is (near) zero or negative.
```

<sup>Created on 2024-02-14 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The example above had two errors and so may be different from your case, but it does the have the error about variance. You can try converting dim_pb3 to a matrix by as.matrix() and see whether you still have the error message.

By the way, you mentioned that you are "working with the pooled covariance matrix after multiple imputation using mice." Just curious. Should cfai.mi() from semTools be used in this case?

https://rdrr.io/cran/semTools/man/runMI.html

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Although I keep the imputed datasets the same, I get different model fit indices and test statistics every time I run the cfa.mi models with imputed categorical Data.
messages.subject_clean: Although I keep the imputed datasets the same, I get different model fit indices and test statistics every time I run the cfa.mi models with imputed categorical Data.
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am trying to test the Measurement Invariance in my one-latent-factor model. I have 24 questions coded "correct" and "incorrect" and 3 different groups in my data (Sample sizes are approximately 200 for each group). Since there is some missing data, as far as I know, I can't run the CFA models with the WLSMV estimator. So, I first imputed the data with Amelia package and then tried to run the cfa.mi function in the semTools package as stated in the runMI function description.
My problem is that every time I run the configural or metric model, fit indices (CFI, TLI, RMSEA) and the model test statistics yield very different results (I keep the imputed datasets the same).

Here's the code I am running:
###############################################################
data_mck <- MCK_DATA_
data_mck <- data_mck[,1:32]
set.seed(12345)
Amelia.imputation <- amelia(data_mck[,-c(14,15,16,17,18)],  m = 20, idvars = "ID",  ords = c("Q1","Q2A","Q3A","Q3B","Q3C","Q5","Q6","Q8A","Q8B","Q8C","Q10","Q12B","Q13A","Q13B","Q13C","Q17A","Q18B","Q19A","Q19B","Q19C","Q19D","Q20A","Q22","Q23"), p2s = FALSE, incheck = T)
imps_mck <- Amelia.imputation$imputations
## here I had 20 imputed datasets with 24 binary questions ###
for (i in 1: 20) { imps_mck[[i]]$COUNTRY <- factor(imps_mck[[i]]$COUNTRY) }
### There are 3 different groups (countries) in the dataset ###
model_mck <- 'MCK =~ Q1+Q2A+Q3A+Q3B+Q3C+Q5+Q6+Q8A+Q8B+Q8C+Q10+Q12B+Q13A+Q13B+Q13C+Q17A+Q18B+Q19A+Q19B+Q19C+Q19D+Q20A+Q22+Q23'
cfa.configural <- cfa.mi(model_mck, data = imps_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "COUNTRY", ordered = TRUE)
summary(cfa.configural, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

cfa.metric <- cfa.mi(model_mck, data =  imps_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "COUNTRY", ordered = TRUE,
group.equal = "loadings")
summary(cfa.metric.amelia_mck_wout_Q9, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

cfa.scalar<- cfa.mi(model_mck, data = imps_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "COUNTRY", ordered = TRUE,
group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts"))
summary(cfa.scalar, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

### All models give very different and inconsistent fit indices and test statistics when I delete them from the R environment and re-run them ###

lavTestLRT.mi(cfa.metric, h1=cfa.configural)
###############################################################

Is there anything I am doing wrong with the codes? I couldn't find any information in the group chats and other platforms. It would be very appreciated if someone could take a look and help.
Many thanks in advance. I wish everyone a productive and beautiful day.
Best Wishes,
Enes.

10 Nisan 2020 Cuma tarihinde saat 00:31:36 UTC+2 itibarıyla Terrence Jorgensen şunları yazdı:

> > I am still running into the same error as I was before: "Error in data[, var1] : incorrect number of dimensions".
>
> My fault, I overlooked the fact that you would be calling the same list in indProd() instead of the first argument simply being each data.frame within the list.
>
> I have added part of the following example to the ?indProd help page for future reference:
>
> HSMiss <- HolzingerSwineford1939[ , c(paste("x", 1:9, sep = ""),
>                                       "ageyr","agemo","school")]
> set.seed(12345)
> HSMiss$x5 <- ifelse(HSMiss$x5 <= quantile(HSMiss$x5, .3), NA, HSMiss$x5)
> age <- HSMiss$ageyr + HSMiss$agemo/12
> HSMiss$x9 <- ifelse(age <= quantile(age, .3), NA, HSMiss$x9)
> library(Amelia)
> set.seed(12345)
> HS.amelia <- amelia(HSMiss, m = 3, noms = "school", p2s = FALSE)
> imps <- HS.amelia$imputations
> imps <- lapply(imps, indProd,
>                var1 = c("x1","x2","x3"), var2 = c("x4","x5","x6"))
> ## specify CFA model from lavaan's ?cfa help page
> HS.model <- '
>   visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>   textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>   VT =~ x1.x4 + x2.x5 + x3.x6
>   speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
>   speed ~ visual + textual + VT
> '
> out <- cfa.mi(HS.model, data = imps, std.lv = TRUE)
> summary(out)
>
>
> For your case, you can use:
>
> impmitml <- lapply(impmitml, indProd,
>                    var1=6:8, var2=5, match = FALSE)
>
> Sorry for the confusion (and delayed reply).  Also, in case you were planning to use the probing functions in semTools, they now work with lavaan.mi objects in the latest development version (0.5-2.921)
>
> devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")
>
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Prof. Brown,

First of all, thank you for taking the time to respond. I understand that it's a simulation research and the reason for iterations is to minimise the standard errors. However, this much variation in the results makes me unconfident about running the models and presenting the results. For example, when I run 2 identical configural models with the same imputed datasets at different times, one model gives test statistics of 1475.530 with an 1131 df, and 0.558 CFI, 0.524 TLI, 0.039 RMSEA fit statistics whereas the other model gives the test statistics of 1279.201 with 1131 df, and 0.906 CFI, 0.899 TLI, 0.026 RMSEA fit statistics. Is this much variation normal?
On this point, should I interpret these results as cfa models are not reliable when used with my data, thus it is not convenient to use it to test the measurement invariance?
Or should I just pick the best-fit model and report its results in my thesis?

dear Enes
the difference in x2 of 200 points seems like a lot. But again I remember you said n=200 so this might not be too much given the size of the standard errors. Search out what other people have found in simulation studies with n of that size.
It seems that RMSEA and CFI are sensitive to model specification, model complexity, and sample sizes. So the problem could be related to those being unstable estimators. see
Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864
i would calculate the M and SD of the parameters across the multiple runs, to see where the central tendency lies. If the 95%CI does not include positive values then maybe the problem is N or it could be your model or it could be you need to run 1000 iterations.
You can't reach any conclusions based on the 2 data points you report.
best wishes

This is strange because you used set.seed(). The imputation, though "random," should still be reproducible. I simulated a dataset (though see my comment on COUNTRY, which I do not know how it was stored in the original data) and ran a modified version of your code:

p <- length(vnames)
set.seed(12345)
rho <- matrix(.6, p, p)
diag(rho) <- 1
data_mck <- MASS::mvrnorm(600, rep(0, p), rho)
data_mck[data_mck > 0] <- 1
data_mck[data_mck <= 0] <- 0

May you share more about your dataset such that we can accurately simulate the format (not the data) of the dataset you are using, so we can see why the results changed every time you run the code?

If I misunderstood your scenario, sorry about that.

-- Shu Fai

P.S.: The test statistics you got "may" be different from mine even if you run the same code in your compute because it may depend on the random number generator. Butt the results should still be reproducible when run several times on the same machine.

messages.body_plain:
I believe it is safe to use only ordered = TRUE and let's lavaan set other options for us, as explained below in the last paragraph:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

If we manually set the estimator (e.g., estimator = "DWLS"), then this overrides the default behavior and lavaan expects us to set other options, such as the methods used for the SEs (the "se" argument) and the model test statistics (the "test" argument). We can do this if we want to fully specify the methods to be used. Otherwise, let lavaan set them.

This is an illustration, showing the differences (some differences are also printed by summary(), e.g., in the section "Parameter Estimates:"):  Parameter Estimates:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-17
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
dat <- HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)]
dat <- scale(dat)
dat[dat > 0] <- 1
dat[dat <= 0] <- 0
dat <- as.data.frame(dat)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit1 <- cfa(HS.model, data = dat, ordered = TRUE)
fit2 <- cfa(HS.model, data = dat, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "DWLS")

# Same estimator
lavInspect(fit1, "options")$estimator
#> [1] "DWLS"
lavInspect(fit2, "options")$estimator
#> [1] "DWLS"
# Robust test statistics only in fit1
names(lavInspect(fit1, "test"))
#> [1] "standard"       "scaled.shifted"
names(lavInspect(fit2, "test"))
#> [1] "standard"
# Different methods for standard errors
lavInspect(fit1, "options")$se
#> [1] "robust.sem"
lavInspect(fit2, "options")$se
#> [1] "standard"
```

<sup>Created on 2024-02-19 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan community,

We are trying to run a serial mediation model based on imputed data set. However, we’re facing a strange situation, we will be much appreciated for any suggestions.

We have two mediators (M1, M2), one independent variables (X), one dependent variables (Y).

We first did multiple imputation in R using mice package, and then we defined mediation model as follows:

Model <- “M1 ~ a1 * X

M2 ~ a2 * X + d21 * M1

Y ~  cp * X + b1  * M1 + b2 * M2

ind_eff := a1*d21*b2”

Then we used the sem.mi() function:

sem.mi(Model, data_imputed)

fit <-sem.mi(model, dat_mut_IMP)

summary(fit,  standardized = T, fit.measures = T, test = "D2")

Then we got a warning of “Error in if (categorical.flag) { : argument is of length zero”.  Further, we can not obtain the parameter outputs, like path coefficents. Very appreciated for your help.

Many thanks in advance for your time

Best,
Tuan & Kexin

Thank you again for your help.
Yours sincerely,
Enes.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the clarification. This is strange because, with set.seed() used, the imputation results are supposed to be reproducible. For cfa.mi(), same data, same results. There should be no random process in the optimization in lavaan.

When you run the code, these two lines should always be run together:

set.seed(12345)
Amelia.imputation <- amelia(data_mck[,-c(14,15,16,17,18)],  m = 20, idvars = "ID",  ords = c("Q1","Q2A","Q3A","Q3B","Q3C","Q5","Q6","Q8A","Q8B","Q8C","Q10","Q12B","Q13A","Q13B","Q13C","Q17A","Q18B","Q19A","Q19B","Q19C","Q19D","Q20A","Q22","Q23"), p2s = FALSE, incheck = T)

Before you run cfa.mi(), you can check the imputed datasets to make sure they are indeed the same dataset. E.g., this checks the first imputed dataset:

summary(imps_mck[[1]])

You did mention that you kept the imputed datasets the same but it does no harm to check again before running cfa.mi(), just in case.

If imps_mck is indeed the same before running cfa.mi(), then, as far as I understand, for the same computer, you should see the same results.

If you confirmed that, right before running cfa.mi(), imps_mck is the same, but then the cfa.mi() results are different, then something's wrong.

-- Shu Fai

El lunes, 12 de febrero de 2024 a las 13:06:04 UTC-6, Jošt Bartol escribió:
> Hi,
>
> The robust version of fit indicators for estimator DWLS and similar was introduced only with version 0.6-13 of lavaan. As it says there (https://www.lavaan.ugent.be/history/dot6.html) it computes robust fit indices only if ALL data are categorical. I think I read somewhere there is a work around (maybe search for it on this forum), but when I tried it (quite some time ago) I still didn't get the robust version.
>
> As for multi group analysis. The output is simply saying that you have to report the scaled/robust chi-square (find in the model output) and not the chi-square that is reported as part of multigroup testing. The warning is because you are trying to compare models with the same degrees of freedom - which is not possible.
> Related to the mutli group analysis. In Model 5, although you include Pa ~  Be you still have the same degrees of freedom because you are replacing Pa ~~  Be. For measurement invariance, you are trying to test equality of factor loadings which you don't have (path analysis).
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> Best,
> Jošt

messages.subject: Measurement invariance for binary categorical data and continous together: are there any special considerations?
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance for binary categorical data and continous together: are there any special considerations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have read in this group (also checked Wu and Estabrook, 2016) that when an observed variable has only one threshold (it is binary) we cannot distinguish threshold, loading and intercept for measurement invariance in multiple group comparisons. So we have to constraint everything at once and test scalar invariance and compare it to the baseline model. But here I wonder whether this applies for cases where there are binary data and continous. Specifically, I am trying to compare this path analysis model across groups:

So, I wonder whether I should consider some steps to account for the continous part of the model. Do you know? What is the correct approach for the cases when you have binary data and continous all in the same model.

Thanks!

Hi everyone,

I will run a moderated mediation analysis (Hayes, model 15) and compare the model between two groups for my PhD.

I run the following code, however, I could not see the index of modmed. Also, I'm not sure if the code is useful for my model since I'm a newbie in R. I read the document in the link Chapter 15: Moderated Mediation <https://ademos.people.uic.edu/Chapter15.html#5_moderated_mediation_analyses_using_%E2%80%9Clavaan%E2%80%9D_package>. Before running the analysis, I calculate centered score for IV, MOD and MED, then create interaction term for IV:MOD and MED:MOD. In structural model, I added these interaction terms directly, and used centered variables, except DV. All my variables are continues. Besides, I import my data via "haveen" button, not the code. My data set name is "IntOrnek" and grouping variable is "country" coded as 1, 2. In sum, is there anyone who can help me writing the correct code? I found another package useful for moderated mediation however I'm not sure if I can run multigroup SEM in that packages.
Lastly, I run the code, got the output, there is no index of modmed and direct, indirect, total and proportion of mediation

I would be grateful if anyone could help me.

Thanks in advance

library(lavaan)

> Model15 <- '
MED ~ a1*IV
 DV ~ cdash1*IV + cdash2*MOD + cdash3*MOD:IV + b1*MED  + b2*MOD:MED  '

# MOD   ~  MOD .mean*1
MOD   ~  MOD .mean * 1

# MOD ~~ MOD .var*MOD
MOD ~ ~ MOD .var*MOD

# Indirect effects conditional on moderator
indirect.SDbelow =~ (a1 + a3*( MOD .mean-sqrt( MOD.var))) * b1
indirect.SDabove =~ (a1 + a3*( MOD.mean+sqrt(MOD.var))) * b1

# Direct effects conditional on moderator
direct.SDbelow =~  cdash1 + cdash3*( MOD.mean-sqrt(MOD.var))
direct.SDabove =~  cdash1 + cdash3*( MOD.mean+sqrt(MOD.var))

# Total effects conditional on moderator
total.SDbelow =~  direct.SDbelow + indirect.SDbelow
total.SDabove =~  direct.SDabove + indirect.SDabove

# Proportion mediated conditional on moderator
prop.mediated.SDbelow =~  indirect.SDbelow / total.SDbelow
prop.mediated.SDabove =~  indirect.SDabove / total.SDabove

## Ensure country variable is character
IntOrnek$country <- as.character(IntOrnek$country)  # Add this line

# Fit the multigroup model
Model15Sem <- sem(Model15, data = IntOrnek, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML", group = "country")

Model15Sem.constrained <- sem(Model15, data =  IntOrnek, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML", group = "country", group.equal = c("regressions"))

summary(Model15Sem, modindices = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

All the lines that define new parameters should be included in the model syntax. From the message, it seems that the model syntax end at " b2*MOD:MED", with a single quote at the end of that line.

Moreover, for lines like the following ones, I believe you mean ":=", not "=~".

indirect.SDbelow =~ (a1 + a3*( MOD .mean-sqrt( MOD.var))) * b1

You can see an example here:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

You may encounter other issues when you ask for standardized solution. The following thread is not about mediation, but the same issue may occur in some models with indirect effects.

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/AWGORQnmKBg/m/ZohckNBFAQAJ

But the problems with the model syntax should be fixed first.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

Different from the question above, I will run model 15 which moderator has an impact on x to y path. My data set name is IntOrnek and the grouping variable is country. Variables are X (predictor), Y(outcome), M (mediator between X-Y), V(moderator between X-Y and M-Y). Path names are as following:
X -> Y  "c1"
X -> M "a"
M -> Y "b1"
V -> Y  "c2"
VM -> Y "b2"
VX -> Y "c3"

According to that, I wrote the following,
model15 <- ' M ~ a*X
           Y ~ c1*X + b1*M + c2*V + b2*VM + c3*VX
           conditional indirect := a(b1 + b2*V)
           conditional direct := c1 + c3*V
           total :=  a(b1 + b2*V) +  c1 + c3*V
           index.mod.med := a*b2*c3        #Should I add “b2” as well? is the correct calculation multiplication or addiction?
           Vlow := a*b1 + a*b2*c3*-0.5  # If the previous index calculation correct
   Vhigh := a*b1 + a*b2*c3*0.5
   V ~ V.mean * 1
           V ~~ V.var * V
   total.SDbelow :=  direct + indirect
# Ensure country variable is character
   IntOrnek$country <- as.character(IntOrnek$country)'
 # Fit the multigroup model
> Model15Sem <- sem(Model15, data = IntOrnek, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML", group = "country")

Does it make sense to compare two samples in terms of the model and effect of the moderator? I am not sure if I have written the indirect and conditional effect codes correctly. Since I am new to R, I find it difficult to interpret the examples I find and adapt them to my model. None of the examples have a moderator on the c' path.

Any contribution would be greatly appreciated.
Thanks in advance.

messages.subject: Re: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.subject_clean: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.body_plain:
Terrence,

Thank you very much for your reply and sorry for the delay in getting back to you.

I was not aware that models that treat exogenous variables as fixed are actually estimating covariance.
I think I understand why lavaan defaults to `fixed.x=FALSE`.

I really appreciate it.
2024年1月11日木曜日 21:52:47 UTC+9 Terrence Jorgensen:

> > The definition of the independence model that I learned from some introductory-level textbooks is a model that assumes that there is no covariance between variables (therefore it estimates only variances).
> Yes, among endogenous variables.  It was proposed in the context of "full SEM" (really, the first incremental fit index was developed for factor analysis), not path analysis among observed variables.  Most authors don't explain this very carefully when they make overgeneralizing statements about the independence model.
>
> > However, when a model is fitted with fixed.x = FALSE (i.e. model estimates variances and covariances) the independence model seems to estimate covariances, and those covariances are counted as free parameters.
> This has nothing to do with fixed.x=FALSE.  Those covariances will be nonzero by default even when fixed.x=TRUE.  I don't have access to your data, so here is a reprex:
>
> library(lavaan)
>
> ## Fit regression model twice, treating exogenous variables as fixed or random variables:
>
> fitF <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = FALSE)
> fitT <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = TRUE)
>
> In the first case, the predictors are considered random variables, so their (co)variances are estimated, as indicated by nonzero numbers in the $free column
>
> data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitF))
>
>   id lhs op rhs user block group free   ustart exo
> 1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.358370   0
> 2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    2 1.381784   0
> 3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    3 1.274865   0
> 4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    4       NA   0
>
> In the second case, the predictors are considered fixed variables, so their (co)variances are not estimated, as indicated by zeros in the $free column (and ones in the $exo column).  Instead, those values (both variances and the covariance) are fixed to their observed (nonzero!) sample statistics, reflecting the assumption that in any future replication of this study, the same summary statistics would be observed due to using the same sampling methodology.
>
> data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitT))
>   id lhs op rhs user block group free    ustart exo
> 1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.3583698   0
> 2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    0 1.3817839   1
> 3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 1.2748649   1
> 4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 0.4510639   1
>
> The reason that observed predictors' covariances can be nonzero (whether estimated or fixed) in the independence model is that there are typically no hypotheses about those parameters.  By definition, exogenous variables are not explained in the model (they only do the explaining), so it would be inconsistent to place those restrictions in a "worst fitting, but still theoretically defensible" model.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Re: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.subject_clean: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.body_plain:
I really like this paper by Widaman and Thompson, that talks about some of the complexities of null models.  It's not completely unambiguous what the null model should be, and it's not impossible for the null to have a lower chi-square than the fitted model (which I would have told you was impossible before I read this paper.)

https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2003-00272-005

On Mon, 26 Feb 2024 at 04:51, mi nigi <nigimi...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Terrence,
>
> Thank you very much for your reply and sorry for the delay in getting back to you.
>
> I was not aware that models that treat exogenous variables as fixed are actually estimating covariance.
> I think I understand why lavaan defaults to `fixed.x=FALSE`.
>
> I really appreciate it.
> 2024年1月11日木曜日 21:52:47 UTC+9 Terrence Jorgensen:
> > >
> > > The definition of the independence model that I learned from some introductory-level textbooks is a model that assumes that there is no covariance between variables (therefore it estimates only variances).
> > Yes, among endogenous variables.  It was proposed in the context of "full SEM" (really, the first incremental fit index was developed for factor analysis), not path analysis among observed variables.  Most authors don't explain this very carefully when they make overgeneralizing statements about the independence model.
> >
> > > However, when a model is fitted with fixed.x = FALSE (i.e. model estimates variances and covariances) the independence model seems to estimate covariances, and those covariances are counted as free parameters.
> > This has nothing to do with fixed.x=FALSE.  Those covariances will be nonzero by default even when fixed.x=TRUE.  I don't have access to your data, so here is a reprex:
> >
> > library(lavaan)
> >
> > ## Fit regression model twice, treating exogenous variables as fixed or random variables:
> >
> > fitF <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = FALSE)
> > fitT <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = TRUE)
> >
> > In the first case, the predictors are considered random variables, so their (co)variances are estimated, as indicated by nonzero numbers in the $free column
> >
> > data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitF))
> >
> >   id lhs op rhs user block group free   ustart exo
> > 1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.358370   0
> > 2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    2 1.381784   0
> > 3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    3 1.274865   0
> > 4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    4       NA   0
> >
> > In the second case, the predictors are considered fixed variables, so their (co)variances are not estimated, as indicated by zeros in the $free column (and ones in the $exo column).  Instead, those values (both variances and the covariance) are fixed to their observed (nonzero!) sample statistics, reflecting the assumption that in any future replication of this study, the same summary statistics would be observed due to using the same sampling methodology.
> >
> > data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitT))
> >   id lhs op rhs user block group free    ustart exo
> > 1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.3583698   0
> > 2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    0 1.3817839   1
> > 3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 1.2748649   1
> > 4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 0.4510639   1
> >
> > The reason that observed predictors' covariances can be nonzero (whether estimated or fixed) in the independence model is that there are typically no hypotheses about those parameters.  By definition, exogenous variables are not explained in the model (they only do the explaining), so it would be inconsistent to place those restrictions in a "worst fitting, but still theoretically defensible" model.
> >
> > Terrence D. Jorgensen
> > Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> > Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> > http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
> >

messages.body_plain:
> One issue I have is that groups 1 and 3 all have the same level of education (no variance in years of education). Is it possible to specify that education should only predict cognition in groups 2 and 4?

Fixing the slope to zero in groups 1 and 3 won't work because the sample covariance matrix is NPD when there is zero variance.

Instead, you can use the block-style syntax to specify separate models per group.  Then you can just leave the variable out of groups 1 and 3 but include it in groups 2 and 4.

There is an example of such a model here:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/uyq3h0wXh6g

messages.subject: Multiple Groups with Constrained Lavaan Model
messages.subject_clean: Multiple Groups with Constrained Lavaan Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently running the fixed RI-CLPM model from Haymaker with constrained auto-regressive and cross lagged relations over time (shown below). I now want to test “sex” as a potential moderator.  Would this involve comparing a version of the RI-CLPM in which there are no constraints across the groups, with a modified version of the model in which the lagged regression coefficients are constrained across the groups? If so, how would I need to modify the model below to achieve this.

Thank you in advance,
Maya

RICLPM2 <- '
  # Create between components (random intercepts)
  # RIx =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4 + 1*x5
  # RIy =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4 + 1*y5

  RIx =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
  RIy =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4

  # Create within-person centered variables
  wx1 =~ 1*x1
  wx2 =~ 1*x2
  wx3 =~ 1*x3
  wx4 =~ 1*x4
  # wx5 =~ 1*x5
  wy1 =~ 1*y1
  wy2 =~ 1*y2
  wy3 =~ 1*y3
  wy4 =~ 1*y4
  # wy5 =~ 1*y5

  # Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
  wx2 ~ a*wx1 + b*wy1
  wy2 ~ c*wx1 + d*wy1
  wx3 ~ a*wx2 + b*wy2
  wy3 ~ c*wx2 + d*wy2
  wx4 ~ a*wx3 + b*wy3
  wy4 ~ c*wx3 + d*wy3
  # wx5 ~ a*wx4 + b*wy4
  # wy5 ~ c*wx4 + d*wy4

  # Estimate covariances between residuals of within-person centered variables
  # (i.e., innovations)
  wx2 ~~ wy2
  wx3 ~~ wy3
  wx4 ~~ wy4
  # wx5 ~~ wy5

  # Estimate covariance between within-person centered variables at first wave
  wx1 ~~ wy1 # Covariance

  # Estimate variance and covariance of random intercepts
  RIx ~~ RIx
  RIy ~~ RIy
  RIx ~~ RIy

  # Estimate (residual) variance of within-person centered variables
  wx1 ~~ wx1 # Variance
  wy1 ~~ wy1
  wx2 ~~ wx2 # Residual variance
  wy2 ~~ wy2
  wx3 ~~ wx3
  wy3 ~~ wy3
  wx4 ~~ wx4
  wy4 ~~ wy4
  # wx5 ~~ wx5
  # wy5 ~~ wy5
'
 ( RICLPM2.fit <- lavaan(RICLPM2,
                           data = dat2,
                           missing = 'ML',
                           group = "demo_sex_v2.1",
                           meanstructure = T,
                           int.ov.free = T
)

Maya--
     Yes, your understanding is correct. With a discrete moderator (if you treat "sex" this way), then differences in parameter values across groups imply moderation effects.
     As is general with lavaan, if there is one way to do something, there are actually several ways to do it. To allow for different effects in two groups, replace the single labels for individual parameters with two labels within a c() operator. So this line of your code:

wx2 ~ a*wx1 + b*wy1

would become

wx2 ~ c(a.m, a.f)*wx1 + c(b.m, b.f)*wy1

if you wanted to code the two sex groups as "m" and "f." Remember that, in lavaan syntax, a period (.) is just another character. Some people recommend underscore (_) for better readability.

     This coding suggests two different values for each parameter estimate. To explicitly specify equality across groups, you might end your syntax with a series of equality statements, using the == operator, as in:

a.m == a.f
b.m == b.f

So you would have one general batch of syntax for both instances (constrained and not constrained) and then the additional lines for the model constraining parameter estimates to equality. Or you could comment out (using #) the equality constraints in the version allowing the estimates to be free across groups.

If so, how would I need to modify the model below to achieve this.
>
> Thank you in advance,
> Maya
>
> RICLPM2 <- '
>   # Create between components (random intercepts)
>   # RIx =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4 + 1*x5
>   # RIy =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4 + 1*y5
>
>   RIx =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
>   RIy =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4
>
>   # Create within-person centered variables
>   wx1 =~ 1*x1
>   wx2 =~ 1*x2
>   wx3 =~ 1*x3
>   wx4 =~ 1*x4
>   # wx5 =~ 1*x5
>   wy1 =~ 1*y1
>   wy2 =~ 1*y2
>   wy3 =~ 1*y3
>   wy4 =~ 1*y4
>   # wy5 =~ 1*y5
>
>   # Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
>   wx2 ~ a*wx1 + b*wy1
>   wy2 ~ c*wx1 + d*wy1
>   wx3 ~ a*wx2 + b*wy2
>   wy3 ~ c*wx2 + d*wy2
>   wx4 ~ a*wx3 + b*wy3
>   wy4 ~ c*wx3 + d*wy3
>   # wx5 ~ a*wx4 + b*wy4
>   # wy5 ~ c*wx4 + d*wy4
>
>   # Estimate covariances between residuals of within-person centered variables
>   # (i.e., innovations)
>   wx2 ~~ wy2
>   wx3 ~~ wy3
>   wx4 ~~ wy4
>   # wx5 ~~ wy5
>
>   # Estimate covariance between within-person centered variables at first wave
>   wx1 ~~ wy1 # Covariance
>
>   # Estimate variance and covariance of random intercepts
>   RIx ~~ RIx
>   RIy ~~ RIy
>   RIx ~~ RIy
>
>   # Estimate (residual) variance of within-person centered variables
>   wx1 ~~ wx1 # Variance
>   wy1 ~~ wy1
>   wx2 ~~ wx2 # Residual variance
>   wy2 ~~ wy2
>   wx3 ~~ wx3
>   wy3 ~~ wy3
>   wx4 ~~ wx4
>   wy4 ~~ wy4
>   # wx5 ~~ wx5
>   # wy5 ~~ wy5
> '
>  ( RICLPM2.fit <- lavaan(RICLPM2,
>                            data = dat2,
>                            missing = 'ML',
>                            group = "demo_sex_v2.1",
>                            meanstructure = T,
>                            int.ov.free = T
> )
>

messages.subject: Re: Adding a covariate to EFA, and get traditional EFA results
messages.subject_clean: Adding a covariate to EFA, and get traditional EFA results
messages.body_plain:
I understand that what you need is to add an observable exogenous variable as a covariate that predicts one or more latent variables, did I get it right?

If that is the case, there are a few things that possibly need to be sorted out first.
In an EFA you don't know for sure how many latent variables you have in advance, nor how to interpret them. If you wanted to add a covariate, you would probably need to "predict all of them at a time" (and then test whether those regression weights are statistically significant). As far as I know, this is not common in EFA and I don't think it can be done in any available software. It might be possible, but at least you would need to specify the number of factors you expect to find (which possibly undermines the purpose of the EFA itself, partially at least).
In a CFA you have a clear idea of what factors you are modelling, how many, and what each of them represents, so it makes better sense to add covariates to predict one or more, and you can easily do it as you already know.
In any case, none of the previous models with covariates added should be understood as a factor-analytic model, as I understand it, but as a Structural Equation Model in the more general sense. The latter case (the CFA) resembles what is usually referred to as a MIMIC model. In the case of the EFA, as I said above, I don't think there is such a thing in the literature, but if there is, it should be probably understood as an "Exploratory SEM" (ESEM), although I think this term is usually reserved to cases where the non-exploratory part of the model only implies correlations among the unique variances of the indicators.
If your concern is how the results are output, you should be able to obtain all of those indicators from the CFA model as well. It may look less familiar and/or require more work, but it is ultimately possible to get them. To my understanding, the criterion for choosing EFA over CFA should be that you do not have a clear theoretical understanding of what is the internal structure representing your data.
I'm sorry that I can't be more helpful. I hope this helps you gain a clearer insight into the problem, in any case.

Best,
Daniel

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>
